answer:
## HEADLINE ANSWER

**Amber's highest value is in the millennium spanning 4000–3001 BCE — the 4th millennium BCE in standard ordinal notation — and it peaked over the interval ~3300–3000 BCE (± one century), in the Middle Neolithic.** This is the highest *relative* amber signal, not the largest absolute quantity.

## Hypothesis (submission-ready)

> Amber shows its highest relative representation in the **4th millennium BCE (the millennium spanning 4000–3001 BCE)**, where all ten 100-year bins carry z-values of +1.46 to +1.54 (mean z = **+1.48** against a standardised mean of 0.00 and SD of 1.00 for the whole 4300–500 BCE frame). The series reaches its maximum of **z = +1.54 in four consecutive bins, giving a peak interval of 3300–3000 BCE**, inside a broader, sharply bounded highstand of **z ≥ +1.46 from 4000 to 3000 BCE**. The next-highest value anywhere else in the entire 3800-year record is only +0.37, so the winner and runner-up millennia (mean z = −0.15) do not overlap in value at all — a margin of ~1.6 SD. Culturally, the peak falls entirely within the **Middle Neolithic (MN, 3400–3000 BCE)**, the highest of all six periods (mean z = +1.52); the highstand begins in the Early Neolithic (EN) and ends abruptly at the **MN→Single Grave (SG) transition, collapsing from +1.54 at 3000 BCE to +0.37 at 2900 BCE**, after which amber never again exceeds +0.37 in the following 2400 years. I therefore hypothesise that amber's importance was a specifically Early/Middle Neolithic phenomenon in this region, culminating in the middle centuries of the 4th millennium BCE and terminating at the onset of the 3rd millennium, rather than being linked to later metallurgical exchange networks. This is a descriptive claim about standardised relative frequency within the 4300–500 BCE frame; the data carry no error bars or counts, so the peak cannot be tested for statistical significance, and no claim is made about amber after 500 BCE.

## Two corrections to your reporting instruction 1 — important

**My plan-phase claim that "the winner is the 4th millennium under both conventions" was wrong.** My plan's `loose` function, `(b-1)//1000+1`, is algebraically identical to strict `ceil(b/1000)` — I had never actually tested the alternative. Corrected:

| Convention | Winner label for bins 4000–3001 BCE | Mean z | Runner-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 ordinal, standard (4th = 4000–3001) | **4th millennium BCE** | +1.484 | 3rd, −0.148 |
| S2 rounded (4th = 3999–3000) | **4th millennium BCE** | +1.492 | 3rd, −0.409 |
| S3 *your* example (3000–2000 = 4th) | **5th millennium BCE** | +1.484 | 4th, −0.148 |

So under your stated example convention the same bins are the **5th** millennium — it relabels the *whole* millennium, not merely "the century assigned to the boundary year." I therefore did **not** assert "4th" unqualified: I led with the numeric span **4000–3001 BCE** (convention-free) and gave "4th millennium BCE" as the standard name, since that is what a reader will assume. Two of three conventions say 4th; the robust fact is the bin set. Tell me if you want S3 treated as authoritative instead.

Also corrected: my plan's "invariant winning bin set" was overstated. S1 selects bins 4000–3100, S2 selects 3900–3000 — the 10-bin window shifts by one bin. What *is* invariant is that every convention selects the 4000–3000 BCE plateau and never any other.

## Peak as an interval (instruction 2), with bin-edge caveat

- **(a) Tied maximum:** z = 1.54 at bins 3300, 3200, 3100, 3000 BCE → **interval 3300–3000 BCE**. The maximum is genuinely *tied* across bins, so a single peak year would be an artefact of interpolation, not a data feature.
- **(b) Highstand:** z ≥ 1.46 across **4000–3000 BCE** (11 consecutive bins); next-highest value outside it is +0.37 — a clean, isolated plateau.
- **(c) Smoothed mode:** 300-yr → 3150 BCE; 500-yr → 3243 BCE; both inside the tied-max interval. The 1000-yr window (too wide for 39 points) drags the mode early to 3493 BCE, so I report ≤500-yr windows only.
- **Caveat:** the BCE column's bin semantics are undocumented (does "3300" mean 3300–3201 or 3399–3300 BCE?), so the interval carries ± one century of edge uncertainty. `Amber_inter` is verified to be *exactly* a linear interpolation of the 100-year values (max abs diff 2.2e−16), so it cannot refine the peak below 100 years.

## Cultural-period overlay (instruction 3)

| Period | Span | Mean z | Max z |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MN** | 3400–3000 BCE | **+1.524** | 1.54 |
| EN | 4300–3500 BCE | +0.617 | 1.46 |
| SG | 2900–2300 BCE | −0.223 | 0.37 |
| OBA | 1600–1200 BCE | −0.272 | −0.01 |
| YBA | 1100–500 BCE | −0.706 | −0.58 |
| LN | 2200–1700 BCE | −0.880 | −0.39 |

Peak interval is entirely **MN**; highstand runs EN→MN; collapse at MN→SG (−1.17 z in one bin).

## Robustness and method
Primary series `capital.csv Zamber` (39 bins, no NaNs); `Amber` matches it on all 37 shared bins with max diff 0.0, confirming no rescaling. **Leave-one-bin-out: dropping each of 39 bins in turn never changes the winning millennium (0/39 flips)** — a useful substitute for significance testing given the absence of error bars. Pollen file used as context only (contains no amber column); the amber–openness correlation drops from r=−0.61 (annual, pseudoreplicated) to **r=−0.52 (n=35, honest df)**, with undocumented PC1 sign convention, so it is context and not evidence.

**Limitations:** z-scores are standardised within 4300–500 BCE, so magnitudes are not comparable to amber series standardised elsewhere; only 13 distinct values across 39 bins means the data are likely period-level values propagated onto century bins, so "plateau" may reflect the source aggregation; no counts or errors exist, so nothing is testable; scope is limited to 4300–500 BCE. Three bugs were found and fixed during execution and reported rather than silently patched (the convention-identity bug above, an index-misalignment that made the interpolation check return NaN, and a CE/BCE sign bug that made the pollen join return n=0).

payload.convention_caveat: Ordinal label is NOT convention-invariant: bins 4000-3001 BCE are the 4th millennium BCE under the standard ordinal convention (and under a rounded convention), but become the 5th millennium BCE under the convention '3000-2000 BCE = 4th millennium'. The numeric span and the selected plateau are invariant; only the label and a one-bin shift of the 10-bin window are not.

The next-highest value anywhere else in the record is only +0.37, so the winning and runner-up millennia (mean z = -0.15) do not overlap in value. Culturally the peak falls entirely within the Middle Neolithic (MN, 3400-3000 BCE; mean z = +1.52, highest of six periods), the highstand begins in the Early Neolithic, and it terminates abruptly at the MN -> Single Grave transition (+1.54 at 3000 BCE to +0.37 at 2900 BCE), after which amber never again exceeds +0.37 in 2400 years. Amber's importance was therefore a specifically Early/Middle Neolithic phenomenon culminating in the middle centuries of the 4th millennium BCE, not a feature of later metallurgical exchange networks.
payload.limitation: Descriptive only: z-scores are standardised relative amber signal within the 4300-500 BCE frame (not absolute quantity), bin-edge convention is undocumented (intervals carry ~1 century uncertainty), and there are no counts or error bars so the peak cannot be tested for statistical significance; no claim about amber before 4300 BCE or after 500 BCE.

payload.workflow: 1) Read capital.csv with decimal=','; derived CE=-BCE, calBP=1950+BCE. 2) Verified primary series capital.csv Zamber (39 bins, BCE 4300-500, 100-yr step, 0 NaN, mean 0.0008/sd 1.0014 = standardised within frame). 3) Cross-checked against time_series_data.csv: 37 overlapping century bins, max |Zamber-Amber| = 0.00e+00 -> identical units, no rescaling; Amber only 37/3601 non-null and all on the 100-yr grid; Amber_inter proven to be exactly a linear interpolation of Amber (max abs diff 2.22e-16), so used only as a rolling-window sensitivity. 4) Aggregated mean/max z per calendar millennium under THREE deliberately non-identical labelling conventions (S1 ordinal 4th=4000-3001; S2 rounded 4th=3999-3000; S3 3000-2000=4th) and reported all three. 5) Robustness: leave-one-bin-out over all 39 bins (winner never changes, 0/39 flips). 6) Peak defined as (a) tied-maximum bin set, (b) z>=1.46 highstand, (c) 300/500/1000-yr centred rolling means on Amber_inter. 7) Mapped peak/highstand onto capital.csv cultural periods EN/MN/SG/LN/OBA/YBA. 8) Pollen openness file used as context only (no amber column); amber-openness r reported at both annual (pseudoreplicated, -0.61) and 100-yr-bin (honest df, -0.52) resolution. 9) All tables written to out/, full stdout in out/analysis_log.txt.
